There's a particular hour, just before dawn, when the world seems to belong to no one. The streetlights are still burning but pointless, buzzing over empty roads. The birds haven't started. It's the gap between shifts, the hinge of the night—the hour of nurses, bakers, and insomniacs—and almost everyone else sleeps through it.

I think about how much of the world exists this way: unwitnessed. The spider rebuilding her web at three in the morning after the afternoon rain tore it down. Frost forming on the inside of a barn window. The janitor slowly mopping away a day's worth of footprints, restoring the floor to a blank page no one will thank him for. Somewhere right now, a stranger is finishing a novel that will change their life, and no one will ever know.

We tend to assume the world exists because we see it. It's closer to the truth that the world persists in spite of how little of it we see. Reality happens mostly offstage—in root systems, in the deep ocean, in the private arithmetic of other people's worries. The visible part is the exception.

Maybe that's why small acts of attention feel almost sacred. When you stop to notice the light through a curtain, or really listen to one song all the way through, you're not taking anything from the world. You're witnessing a little of what usually goes unwitnessed. For a moment, that unnoticed thing gets what everything wants, if things want anything at all: to be seen, once, by someone.
